articles.title: Hopwood Hall: DePree's appeal deadline nears after High Court defeat
articles.excerpt: Hopwood DePree has until Wednesday 18 November to seek permission to appeal. Who he is, how he came to Middleton's Hopwood Hall, why the council ended his deal, and what happens next.
articles.content_html:
Hopwood DePree, the American filmmaker who spent seven years trying to save Middleton's Hopwood Hall, has until Wednesday 18 November to decide whether to appeal his High Court defeat.

Any application for permission to appeal must be lodged by that date, although the deadline can be extended to Friday 28 November.

Until the appeal position is settled, Rochdale Council says it cannot move forward with plans for the Grade II* listed hall, which dates back to the 1400s.

Who is Hopwood DePree?

Mr DePree was born in the United States in 1970 and grew up in Holland, Michigan. He worked in Los Angeles as an actor, writer, director and producer, with credits including Doogie Howser, MD and The Last Big Attraction.

His branch of the Hopwood family emigrated to America in the 1700s. He found the hall while researching his family tree online and first visited in 2014, when it was close to collapse.

The Hopwood family lived at the hall until the 1920s. It later became De La Salle College, which closed in 1989, and it has since been owned by the council and stood empty.

How he came to the hall

In 2017 Mr DePree moved to England and signed an option agreement with the council. It gave him the right to buy the hall for a nominal £1 if he could show a viable plan to reinstate and refurbish the whole building.

His plans included a wedding and hospitality venue, a hotel retreat, a gift shop and guided tours. Teams of volunteers worked on the gardens and interior, and he chronicled the restoration on YouTube and in a 2022 memoir, Downton Shabby.

Between 2017 and 2024 the council spent £557,000 on essential repairs, and Historic England put in almost £1 million more. Mr DePree says he has invested more than £750,000 of his own money.

Where the problems began

The agreement was renewed four times. In late October 2024 the council decided not to renew it again, saying its conditions had not been met.

An independent financial consultant had assessed Mr DePree's business model as loss-making and unlikely to attract further public or private funding.

The agreement ended on 31 October 2024 and the site was locked to volunteers. The council said a number of health and safety breaches led it to close the site.

Mr DePree said he found out about the decision from journalists. He maintained he had a legally binding agreement to buy the hall, and by December 2024 about 4,000 people had signed a petition asking the council to let his team return.

He issued a claim against the council in the High Court in September 2025.

The court case

The two-day trial was heard at Manchester Civil Justice Centre on 29 and 30 September 2026.

Mr DePree's barrister, Ashley Bowes, argued that a 2022 planning permission for change of use had triggered his option to buy the hall for £1.

Judge David Hodge KC disagreed. He found the planning application did not cover the whole property or show the ability to reinstate and refurbish the hall, as the option agreement required, and that the council acted lawfully when it ended the agreement.

Mr DePree was ordered to pay £114,000 of the council's legal costs, with £79,000 of that due by 27 October.

What both sides have said

A Rochdale Council spokesperson said after the ruling: "We are pleased with today's judgement. It's a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself."

The spokesperson added: "Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall's long-term future will be considered in due course."

Mr DePree said: "This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK's charitable heritage rescue groups in general."

He added: "We will be watching closely to keep an eye on Rochdale Borough Council's efforts to save Hopwood Hall for the community, and restore it to its former glory."

At a meeting at Rochdale Town Hall on 15 October, council leader Neil Emmott said: "The High Court's judgment in relation to Hopwood Hall does not necessarily mark the end of the legal process."

Cllr Emmott said the council had "bent over backwards" to accommodate Mr DePree, that the £114,000 in costs would be reinvested in the project, and that his "door is always open" if Mr DePree came back with a viable plan.

In an open letter reported on 3 November, Mr DePree said he hoped for "an amicable resolution for Hopwood Hall". He accused the council of taking "an incredibly aggressive legal route of termination".

He asked the council to release its communications, commission an independent review and pause legal proceedings while the two sides talk.

A council spokesperson responded: "We remain focused on securing a sustainable future for Hopwood Hall, once the legal process has concluded."

What happens next

Mr DePree has not said publicly whether he will appeal. His team has said only that it is considering its options.

An appeal can go ahead only with the court's permission. Mr DePree would need to show it has a real prospect of success or that there is another compelling reason for it to be heard.

Cllr Emmott said that if Mr DePree appeals, he would need to pay about £80,000 into court towards the council's costs. "Only Mr DePree and his legal advisers can determine whether an appeal is pursued," he said.

In the meantime the council has completed a £640,000 project to make the roof watertight, finished in December 2025, and says more than £1.6 million has now been spent on the hall by the council and Historic England.

If no appeal is lodged by the deadline, the council says it will consider options for the hall's long-term future and that, once restored, it will be used for the benefit of the wider Middleton community.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council press releases and statements; judgment reported from Manchester Civil Justice Centre; ITV News Granada; BBC; Place North West; Local Government Lawyer; The Manchester Mill. Photograph: Hopwood Hall, Middleton.

articles.title: Laced vapes: what is in them, how they reach children, and how to report sellers
articles.excerpt: Vapes sold to children as cannabis oil are being found to contain spice, a far stronger synthetic drug that has put young people in hospital. Here is what is known and how to report sellers in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Vapes sold to children as cannabis oil are being found to contain spice, a synthetic drug far stronger than the cannabis it imitates, and young people across England have ended up in hospital after using them.

The vapes are usually advertised as “THC” liquid, the active ingredient in cannabis. Dealers swap in spice without telling buyers because it is cheaper, and its strength is unpredictable.

Research by Professor Chris Pudney, of the University of Bath, found in 2025 that as many as one in four vapes confiscated in schools contained spice.

He has identified a network of about 10,000 social media accounts linked to selling it, with “THC vape liquid” advertised for as little as £2. A genuine THC vape typically costs £60 to £80.

In June, ITV News reported the case of a boy who began using what he thought was a THC vape at 12. After about two months of daily use he collapsed, suffered a collapsed lung and spent two weeks in an induced coma.

In Hull, two 13-year-old girls were taken to hospital in April after being handed a vape at a park. Tests found spice and MDMA, according to their mother.

Most of the selling happens on social media, including Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram. Professor Pudney described it as overt drug dealing, with the platforms used as shop windows.

TikTok and Snapchat both say illegal vape sales are banned on their platforms and that they remove such content. Ofcom, which regulates the platforms under the Online Safety Act, says selling drugs to children is illegal and that it will act where platforms fall short.

In Rochdale borough, the council's trading standards team obtained closure orders against six shops in six months to December 2025 for illegal tobacco and vapes, including the Green Shop in Heywood, where illegal vapes were found in the shop and in a car linked to the business.

In June, Rochdale's neighbourhood police and trading standards carried out checks on shops in Milnrow and Littleborough for sales of vapes and alcohol to under-18s, and said the checks would continue regularly.

Parents are advised to warn children never to accept or share a vape from someone they do not know. If a child collapses, has a seizure or struggles to breathe after vaping, call 999.

Information about people selling drugs can be given to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online at gmp.police.uk, or anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Sources: ITV News; University of Bath; Rochdale Borough Council; Greater Manchester Police. Photograph: Rochdale Daily library.

articles.title: Warning issued over e-bikes and e-scooters ahead of Christmas
articles.excerpt: Police warn about the dangers of illegal e-bikes and e-scooters following a tragic incident involving a local teenager.
articles.content_html:
Police have issued a warning to residents about the dangers of purchasing e-bikes and e-scooters this Christmas, following the tragic death of Jacob Calland, a teenager from Rochdale.

Jacob, 16, succumbed to his injuries eight days after an accident involving an e-scooter. His mother, Carly Calland, described her grief, stating that her life has become a 'living nightmare' since losing her son.

She was present when life support was turned off, highlighting the profound impact of this tragedy on her family.

The police's warning comes as part of Operation Hurricane, which targets the anti-social use of off-road bikes and e-scooters. They have cautioned that illegal vehicles could be seized and destroyed, stressing the potential for tragedy associated with their use.

Carly Calland expressed her pain over Jacob's lost future, stating, 'I held him in the hospital before he passed away.' The warning about e-bikes and e-scooters is particularly timely as the festive season approaches, with many considering these vehicles as gifts.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Warning to think twice about buying e-bikes and e-scooters this Christmas - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Warning to think twice about buying e-bikes and e-scooters this Christmas A hard-hitting warning has been issued about the dangers of illegal e-bikes and e-scooters as Christmas approaches. Greater Manchester Police and its partners are urging families to think carefully before buying off-road bikes, illegal e-bikes and e-scooters as Christmas gifts, warning that vehicles used unlawfully could be seized and destroyed — or lead to tragedy. The warning comes as part of Operation Hurricane, GMP’s coordinated crackdown on the anti-social and dangerous use of off-road bikes, e-bikes and quad bikes across Greater Manchester. One family which knows the devastating consequences they can cause is that of Jacob Calland, who died after being hit by a car while he was a passenger on an e-scooter when it went through a red light in Wythenshawe in March this year. He died from his injuries eight days later. Jacob’s mother, Carly Calland, said: “No words will ever be able to describe the pain caused by Jacob’s death. My heart has been smashed into a thousand pieces and there is nothing that can be done to fix it. My life is a living nightmare. “I climbed into the hospital bed to cuddle him and I fell asleep holding him. When I woke up, it was time to turn off the machines. I told Jacob I loved him just before he passed away. My baby boy was gone forever. “He won’t sit his GCSEs, he won’t have his sweet sixteen birthday party, he won’t go to his school prom. He won’t be able to follow his dreams. He won’t get married and won’t have children. His life ended the moment that collision happened.” Jacob and Carly Calland. Image: GMP The e-scooter rider, who was 14 at the time, received an 18-month youth referral order and a five-year driving ban after pleading guilty to causing death by dangerous driving, causing death by driving unlicensed, and causing death by driving uninsured. Following Jacob’s death, Carly launched Jacob’s Journey – a campaign aimed at raising awareness about e-scooter use, their dangers, and the legalities surrounding them. Detective Constable Steve Pennington, of GMP’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said: “This was a tragic incident and one that could have been avoidable. The ongoing efforts of Jacob’s mother, Carly, have been truly commendable and to see her utilising her emotions and grief to power and promote a worthy cause has been inspiring to see. “E-scooters are not harmless toys and they can lead to horrific consequences when used by inexperienced riders and without the due care required. I would urge parents to check what their children are using and to ensure they are educated about the risks of using them on the road.” As Christmas approaches, GMP is reiterating its warning about illegal bikes and scooters. It said: “As we now move towards Christmas, our message is now one of deterrence. Many people purchase these vehicles with good intentions but may not fully understand where they can legally be used or the consequences if they are ridden unlawfully.” Before buying e-bikes and e-scooters as gifts, GMP is reminding people that you can ride an electric bike if you’re 14 or over, and if it is an ‘electrically assisted pedal cycle’ (EAPC). It can be propelled up to a maximum of 15.5mph without pedalling, but only if it has been approved. READ MORE: Volunteers needed to help provide town centre Safe Haven Police seized an e-scooter during a recent operation. Image: GMP Privately owned e-scooters can only be used on private land with the permission of the landowner. Riders should ensure any e-bike complies with Electrically Assisted Pedal Cycle (EAPC) regulations or it may be treated as a motor vehicle in law. Police are also targeting people who use vehicles illegally, ride dangerously, cause anti-social behaviour or use bikes to facilitate criminal activity. Superintendent Mike Russell, of GMP, said: “We are urging families to understand the legal requirements around these vehicles, where they can be ridden and the consequences of using them unlawfully.” “These bikes and scooters can cost a significant amount of money. If the vehicle is being used illegally and is seized, there is a possibility it may be destroyed, leaving families substantially out of pocket. “Our preference is always to educate and prevent rather than enforce, but where vehicles are being used illegally or dangerously, we will take robust action”. Dr David Kung, Clinical Lead of the Paediatric Emergency Department at the Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital, said: “E-bikes and scooters are often much more powerful and faster than parents expect, and we’re seeing an increasing number of children being brought to the Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital Emergency Department because of very severe accidents which have caused life-changing injuries and deaths. An illegal e-bike was seized by undercover police in Middleton town centre in a crackdown on anti-social behaviour. Image: GMP “Our advice is for parents not to buy these as presents at Christmas, where everyone is very excited, but to think very carefully about making sure their children are experienced enough cyclists before getting them an e-bike or e-scooter.” Steve Jordan, Head of Prevention at Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service, said: “E-bikes and e-scooters might sound like an appealing gift this Christmas, but we urge people to think about the risks. “Batteries that have been modified, damaged or used with an incompatible charger can pose a serious fire risk. These fires can develop extremely quickly and, particularly if a vehicle is being charged inside the home or blocking an escape route, the consequences can be devastating. “Our advice is to buy only from a trusted retailer and manufacturer and check for the CE or UKCA safety marking to make sure your battery and charger meet safety standards. “Never charge or store your battery in the hallway, communal area or where it could block your escape in the event of a fire and never leave it charging unattended or while you are asleep.” Anyone concerned about the anti-social use of bikes in their area can report it via gmp.police.uk or by calling 101 or via LiveChat on our website. In an emergency, always call 999. You can read more about the campaign here . SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? We’d love to hear it! Share your news with us. articles.title: Families allege stray firework went into crowd at Heywood Christmas lights switch-on
articles.excerpt: Parents at Heywood's Christmas lights switch-on allege a stray firework went into the crowd this evening, coming within a metre or two of a three-year-old.
articles.content_html:
Families at Heywood's Christmas lights switch-on allege a stray firework went into the crowd this evening, Saturday 14 November, forcing parents with young children to run.

As far as we know, nobody was hurt.

Witnesses believe the display was stopped suddenly because of the alleged stray firework.

One parent said: "We figured it stopped because of the one that went into the crowd (we saw it as it was maybe a meter or two away from my 3 year old). I really think we need an explanation for what happened or some kind of statement and apology. Absolutely beyond disgusted."

Another said: "We were nearly hit by a firework, had to run away with a young child. Think that's why they stopped so abruptly!"

The event itself was extremely well attended, and the newly lit Christmas tree looked spectacular.

Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell, who attended with her child, posted afterwards: "Heywood looks fabulous this evening! Thank you to all of the organisers of today's events and the Christmas lights switch on."

Her post did not mention the alleged stray firework.

Heywood Christmas Lights Switch On, the group behind the event, posted a statement after the display. It did not address the alleged stray firework.

It said: "The Christmas Light Switch On has been organised by the Heywood Business Group for many years along with the 1940s Day, Roch Valley Radio agreed to take on both events however, for the Christmas Lights this year the event had already started being organised by the RDA and council to ensure the event was to go ahead, this meant that it had to meet the councils insurance requirements. We are taking the feedback on how Roch Valley Radio can manage it like the business group at next years event."

The RDA is the Rochdale Development Agency, the council's economic development arm.

In the summer, Heywood Township's delegated sub-committee was asked to put £10,000 towards this year's switch-on, with fireworks and a day of family entertainment. The Rochdale Development Agency was expected to cover the rest of the estimated £12,650 cost.

Rochdale Daily has asked the organisers about the alleged stray firework and what precautions will be taken next year.

Source: eyewitness accounts, a statement from Heywood Christmas Lights Switch On and a public post by Elsie Blundell MP. Photograph: Elsie Blundell MP / Facebook.

articles.title: Middleton Shopping Centre puts on Rochdale's best fireworks display
articles.excerpt: A huge display shot from the roof of Middleton Shopping Centre provided an unforgettable finale to the town's Christmas lights switch-on.
articles.content_html:
Tonight a huge display shot from the roof of Middleton Shopping Centre provided an unforgettable experience for attendees at the town's Christmas lights switch-on.

Set to All I Want for Christmas Is You by Mariah Carey, the fireworks were described by attendees as "absolutely amazing" and "the best display in years".

North Middleton councillor Lee Wolf said: "The lights switch on this year was spectacular - well done, Millie and all those involved in putting this on!"

Millie Taylor is Middleton's town centre manager.

The display closed a day of festivities in Middleton Gardens, which began at noon with food and drink, fairground rides and market stalls including the Teenage Market.

The day's line-up included Middleton Brass Band, community groups, Christmas card making with the Art House and K-pop tribute act The Golden Era of K-POP, ahead of the lights being switched on at 6.30pm.

Broadcaster Michelle Eagleton hosted, joined by cast members from Cinderella, which opens at Middleton Arena on 26 November.

The shopping centre has a long record of backing the town's switch-on.

In 2016 the event was organised by Middleton Town Centre Management, with funding from Middleton Shopping Centre and Middleton Township, the council's committee for the town.

By 2019 it was a joint effort between the shopping centre, town centre management, Middleton Township and Rochdale Borough Council. That year the centre also ran a "Be a Star for a Night" competition to choose a local person to help switch on the lights.

In 2022 the township organised and funded the main event, while the shopping centre organised and sponsored the fireworks finale.

Last year the switch-on was run by the Rochdale Development Agency, the council's economic development arm, and the council billed it as ending with a short fireworks display. The council said it had financially supported the switch-ons in Middleton, Heywood and Littleborough.

Rochdale Daily could not find a published cost for this year's display.

Source: accounts from people who attended and the published event programme. Photograph: supplied.

articles.title: Buckley Hall Prison: drugs, self-harm and ‘requires improvement’
articles.excerpt: Rochdale’s category C prison is meant to send men home sober, skilled and steadier. Inspectors and monitors say drugs, lock-ups and thin education are getting in the way.
articles.content_html:
Analysis

Buckley Hall prison in Rochdale is not doing enough to rehabilitate the roughly 460 men it holds, according to its inspectors and independent monitors.

Prison is a punishment, and it is meant to deter. Few in Rochdale would argue otherwise. But a category C “training” prison has a second job written into its name: to return men to communities like ours able to work, stay sober and cope. The official record suggests Buckley Hall is falling short of that second job.

What the inspectors found

HM Inspectorate of Prisons last made an unannounced inspection of Buckley Hall from 12 to 23 February 2024 and published its report on 20 May 2024. The Chief Inspector found “a slow but perceptible decline” at the prison over recent years.

Inspectors concluded that Buckley Hall was not fulfilling its core function as a training prison. On average, 31% of prisoners were locked in their cells during the working day, and there were not enough places in education, skills and work for the number of men held.

Ofsted, which inspects prison education alongside the inspectorate, rated education, skills and work “requires improvement” overall. Quality of education, personal development, and leadership and management were also rated “requires improvement”. Behaviour and attitudes were rated good. Education at the prison is provided under contract by Novus.

Inspectors said workshop instructors did little to develop men’s English, maths or reading. A new personal development curriculum was too ad hoc to be effective.

Drugs

Drugs were the sharpest concern. The Chief Inspector said well over a quarter of prisoners were active drug takers at the time of the inspection.

Nearly half of the men surveyed (48%) said illicit drugs were easy to get, against 33% at comparable category C prisons. In the previous six months, 27% of random drug tests had come back positive. Only 58% of requested cell searches had been carried out in the previous three months.

The position had not improved a year later. In June 2025 a man died at the prison, and the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman investigated. Its report recorded an average positive random drug test rate of 37% between July 2024 and June 2025, which it called very high.

The same investigation found that drug testing on the prison’s Aspire unit had been reduced because of staff shortages. Intelligence gathered after the man’s death suggested he had owed a debt for psychoactive substances.

The prison’s Independent Monitoring Board (IMB) says drones are not the main problem. Its 2024–25 report says the bigger route is parcels thrown over the fence from a public right of way. Board members also saw identity checks at the gate not always being carried out.

In a letter to the board dated 22 December 2025, prisons minister Lord Timpson said a full enhanced gate security installation at Buckley Hall would need major structural work and is currently unfunded. He said more staff searches, clear bags for staff and stronger identity checks were being used instead.

Self-harm and wellbeing

Inspectors counted 194 self-harm incidents in the 12 months before the 2024 inspection. That was fewer than at similar prisons, but much higher than in 2019 and still rising.

Some 28% of men said they had been on an ACCT plan, the Prison Service’s case-management process for people at risk of suicide or self-harm, against 18% at similar prisons. Only 37% said they could speak to a Listener, a trained prisoner peer supporter, down from 54% in 2019.

The IMB recorded 81 self-harm incidents in the final quarter of its 2024–25 year alone. Kept up for a full year, that pace would equal roughly 700 incidents per 1,000 men, by Rochdale Daily’s calculation. The national rate in men’s prisons was 673 per 1,000 in the year to June 2025.

The board also reported that three men had died in custody at Buckley Hall in 2025 by the time it wrote its report.

Healthcare is one area that has improved. The IMB found a marked improvement in its quality, with nurse-led triage clinics on the wings most days. Physical healthcare is provided by Spectrum Community Health CIC and mental health care by Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust, which includes the Hive, a safe space for men with mental health difficulties.

Spectrum runs clinical drug and alcohol services, with Change Grow Live providing non-clinical recovery support, according to the 2024 inspection report. In June 2025 the drug and alcohol recovery team was working with 180 men, and about 70% of new arrivals signed up for help, according to the IMB.

Anyone affected by the issues in this article can contact Samaritans free, at any time, on 116 123.

Rehabilitation

Inspectors described offending behaviour work as quite limited. The Thinking Skills Programme was replaced by Building Choices in January 2025, and the first group of eight men finished in March 2025.

The Sycamore Tree victim-awareness course has been withdrawn nationally, and a gym instructors’ course was cancelled because of financial constraints, the IMB says.

The Aspire unit can hold up to 60 of the prison’s men serving indeterminate sentences. It is meant to let them progress with less supervision, but inspectors found in 2024 that this was not happening in practice. According to the IMB, 14 men serving IPP sentences were released from Buckley Hall in the first seven months of 2025.

The prison does score well on relationships. Inspectors said excellent relationships between staff and prisoners underpinned much of its success. Some 78% of men knew they had a sentence plan, against 61% at similar prisons, and support for the few men released directly from Buckley Hall was very good.

What prisoners told inspectors

Rochdale Daily could find no published, verifiable first-hand account from a former Buckley Hall prisoner. The clearest public record of prisoners’ views is the inspectorate’s own survey from February 2024.

In it, 56% said complaints were easy to make, down from 78% at the previous inspection in 2019. Only 26% said complaints were dealt with fairly, down from 54%. Some 200 complaints had been rejected when they were submitted for being unsigned, undated or on the wrong form, and many were never resubmitted.

Inspectors judged that weak consultation, complaints and applications processes had undermined the prison’s rehabilitative culture. They also recorded that Buckley Hall had the lowest number of complaints of any category C prison.

How Buckley Hall compares

On violence, Buckley Hall remains one of the calmer category C prisons. Inspectors found violence lower than at most, with fewer serious assaults.

Its “requires improvement” education rating is better than many. The Commons Justice Committee told MPs in November 2025 that 75% of prisons Ofsted inspected in 2024–25 were rated “inadequate” or showed no improvement.

On drugs, it is worse than average. Its 48% “easy to get” figure compares with 33% at comparable category C prisons and 39% across all prisons inspected in 2024–25, according to the Chief Inspector’s annual report.

No robust national positive drug test rate has been published since 2017–18, when it was 21%, according to the National Audit Office. The Chief Inspector says inspectors regularly find rates above 30%. HMP Manchester has recorded 39%, and HMP Hindley near Wigan reached 59% in the six months before inspectors returned in August 2024.

Staffing

In 2024, inspectors found no prison officer vacancies at Buckley Hall. But officers were regularly sent to work at other prisons, so those left behind were redeployed and the daily regime suffered.

By the end of July 2025, the IMB reported 18 staff off sick and four on restricted duties. Wings were locked down on rotation, and gym sessions and religious services were sometimes cancelled.

The men being held have changed too. The IMB describes a much more transient population, with some men arriving with only a short time left to serve, too little to gain workshop experience. Lord Timpson put the prison’s churn rate at around 50% and said Buckley Hall is planned to become a fully category C training prison by 2027.

Nationally, the leaving rate among prison officers was 10.8% in the year to December 2025, down 1.7 percentage points on the year to March 2025, according to HM Prison and Probation Service figures.

Experience is the deeper problem. A Channel 4 FactCheck analysis found 40% fewer officers with at least five years’ service than in 2010. The Prison Reform Trust has said four in ten officers have less than three years’ experience.

Which government ran prisons worst?

The long-run figures do not flatter either party.

Frontline prison officer numbers were cut by around 30% between 2010 and 2013 under the Conservative and Liberal Democrat coalition, when Chris Grayling was Justice Secretary. Assaults reached a record 34,425 in the year to March 2019, under a Conservative government. The national self-harm rate more than doubled, from 310 per 1,000 prisoners in 2010–11 to 699 in the year to March 2019.

Labour took office in July 2024. The self-harm rate peaked at 899 per 1,000 in the year to March 2025, a period spanning both governments. Deaths in custody hit a record 411 in the year to September 2025, entirely under Labour.

The latest figures, published on 29 October 2026, show improvement. Deaths fell 12% to 360 in the year to September 2026, and self-inflicted deaths fell 32% to 66. The self-harm rate fell 10% to 789 per 1,000 in the year to June 2026, and assaults were 5% below their 2019 level.

Measured by violence, the worst year on record came under the Conservatives. Measured by deaths and self-harm, the worst 12-month periods came after Labour took office.

Labour ministers say they inherited a system close to collapse. Justice minister Jake Richards told MPs in January 2026 that at one point in 2024 fewer than 100 places were left across the adult male estate. Critics put the blame on the current government: in October 2025 the Howard League for Penal Reform said the figures showed “the everyday failure presided over by the government”.

What politicians have said

Rochdale MP Paul Waugh (Labour and Co-operative) used a Commons debate on 11 November 2025 to thank officers at Buckley Hall. He said they had “held the line in the face of impossible cuts and challenges” during the previous government’s 14 years.

The Commons Justice Committee, chaired by Hammersmith and Chiswick MP Andy Slaughter, visited Buckley Hall and Greater Manchester probation services and wrote to Lord Timpson about the visit on 12 February 2025. The minister replied on 28 February 2025.

Concerns about staffing at the prison are not new. In 1996, when Group 4 ran Buckley Hall privately, Rochdale’s then Liberal Democrat MP Liz Lynne told the Commons it had one officer for every 3.7 prisoners, against one for every 2.7 at other male category C prisons. The prison returned to public-sector management in 2000.

Rochdale Daily could find no published comment from a Rochdale Borough councillor on conditions at the prison.

When will inspectors return?

No date has been announced, and prison inspections are unannounced. HM Inspectorate of Prisons inspects adult prisons at least once every five years and expects to visit most every two to three years, with Ofsted inspecting education at the same time.

With the last full inspection in February 2024, the next must take place by February 2029 at the latest. On the inspectorate’s usual pattern, it could come at any time.

On the measures its own inspectors and monitors use — time out of cell, drug use, self-harm, education and offending behaviour work — Buckley Hall is not meeting its aims as a training prison.

Rochdale Daily invites comment from the governor of HMP Buckley Hall and HM Prison and Probation Service; from the prison’s contractors Novus, Spectrum Community Health CIC, Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust, Change Grow Live and Amey; from HM Inspectorate of Prisons and Ofsted; and from Rochdale MP Paul Waugh. Responses can be sent to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Animal charity serving Rochdale seeks stallholders for Christmas fairs
articles.excerpt: PAWS is inviting stallholders to apply for December events in Uppermill and Todmorden, supporting a rescue charity whose work includes Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
An animal rescue charity serving Rochdale is inviting stallholders to take part in two Christmas events in December.

Pennine Animal Welfare Society, known as PAWS, has spaces available at its fair in Uppermill on Sunday 6 December and a second event in Todmorden on Saturday 12 December. Wendy Priest, writing on behalf of PAWS, asked interested stallholders to apply by text on 07833 736325.

The Uppermill fair will run from 11am to 3.30pm at the Civic Hall, Lee Street, OL3 6AE. Its supplied poster lists arts and craft stalls, a pop up café, Santa’s grotto, a tombola and a Christmas raffle.

PAWS lists the Todmorden event on its website as a Christmas coffee morning and fair at Central Methodist Church, Union Street, OL14 5AW, from 10.30am to 12.30pm.

Both venues are outside Rochdale borough. The charity’s rescue and rehoming work covers Rochdale as well as neighbouring areas, making the appeal relevant to local makers and traders who want to support an animal welfare organisation working in their community.

The submission does not give stall fees or booking conditions. Applicants can use the charity’s text number to enquire about availability and the terms before booking.

Sources: Wendy Priest for Pennine Animal Welfare Society, submission and event poster supplied on 14 November 2026; PAWS events listing: https://www.pennineanimalwelfaresociety.org/events; charity background: https://www.pennineanimalwelfaresociety.org/our-story

articles.title: Gritters: when & where
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's seven gritters are back out on main roads, bus routes and school streets. Here is when they grit, which roads they cover and where to find a grit bin.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council's gritters are back out across the borough, from Middleton to Littleborough, treating main roads, bus routes and school streets as temperatures fall again.

Councillor Dylan Williams, the council's cabinet member for highways and facilities, said the highways team had already carried out its first full grit of the winter.

Councillor Williams spent an afternoon at the depot with Gavin, one of the service's supervisors, inspecting the fleet of seven gritters and the grit stockpile for this winter.

He said: "We are well prepared. The team conducted the first full grit last night."

When the gritters go out

The council says it usually grits in the evening from about 6.30pm, or in the morning at about 4.30am, when the grit works best.

It avoids rush hours because gritters get stuck in traffic, and sometimes waits for rain to stop so the grit is not washed away.

Councillor Williams said the decision to send the gritters out is based on weather stations in Middleton, Norden and Littleborough, and computers that monitor road temperatures.

Cameras also watch several roads around the clock, including Hollin Lane and Blackstone Edge.

"The vehicles are also tracked on a live map so we can see that all of the roads are done and at what times," he said.

"Our team of gritter drivers are out 24/7, including overnight in the early hours of the morning working very hard to keep our Borough moving."

Where they grit

The council has seven planned gritting routes covering roughly 208 miles of road, and each route takes around four hours to complete.

There are around 450 miles of road in the borough, and the council says it cannot afford to grit them all.

Lists of the roads on each route are published on the council's gritting pages at rochdale.gov.uk.

The council asks drivers to avoid double parking at gritting times, as some roads, including Norton Rose and Barn Meadows, are hard for the gritters to get through.

Grit bins

There are more than 700 grit bins on residential streets across the borough, and Councillor Williams said all of them have been restocked for the cold weather.

He said the borough has the largest stock of residential grit bins in Greater Manchester.

The council says anyone can use the salt in the bins on public roads and pavements, including roads that are not on a gritting route.

What comes next

The council plans to release a video next week showing more of how the roads are kept clear.

Gritting updates are posted under #RochdaleGrit on X, and the council's Highways and Engineering Service can be contacted on 0300 303 8879.

Source: Statement from Councillor Dylan Williams, Rochdale Borough Council cabinet member for highways and facilities, supplied to Rochdale Daily; Rochdale Borough Council gritting and winter service pages. Photograph: Councillor Dylan Williams / supplied.

What it means for Rochdale drivers

  • The council usually grits in the evening from about 6.30pm, or in the morning at about 4.30am.
  • The council has seven planned gritting routes covering roughly 208 miles of road.
  • The council says anyone can use the salt in the bins on public roads and pavements, including roads that are not on a gritting route.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
articles.excerpt: A centuries‑old tale that a Lady Eleanor would be “maid, wife and widow in one day” survives in Healey Dell’s visitor guides — but it begins with nineteenth‑century collectors, not medieval paperwork.
articles.summary: A centuries‑old tale that a Lady Eleanor would be “maid, wife and widow in one day” survives in Healey Dell’s visitor guides — but it begins with nineteenth‑century collectors, not medieval paperwork.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — has long been a place that invites stories. One of the most durable tells of a noblewoman, usually named Lady Eleanor, who visits a local fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden; the old woman declares Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow in one day,” and on her wedding night the bridegroom is slain. That sequence is the version most visitors now read on local trails and in guidebooks. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Read closely, however, and the tale’s pedigree is plain: the story appears in the printed record with nineteenth‑century folklore collectors, not in contemporaneous medieval sources. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire preserves a long, romance‑style telling that names the characters, the taper‑by‑blood ritual, and the fatal wedding‑night — Roby collected oral stories and printed them as tradition rather than as archival fact. ([redlectern.com](https://redlectern.com/read/traditions-of-lancashire-volume-2))

Local antiquarians and modern visitor material have since shaped Roby’s account into the familiar local version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s history leaflets and the Industrial Archaeology guide reproduce the narrative and explicitly link it to later local writers such as William Robertson, showing how the story hardened in print and on the trail. Those guides treat the tale as part of the valley’s folkloric landscape rather than as documentary history. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What the archives actually show is different. The Byron family were lords of the manor of Rochdale across centuries and appear in manorial and local histories; those connections help explain why local storytellers might have attached a Byron name to a dramatic local tale. But the printed versions of the prophecy — Roby and later compilers — are not supported by surviving medieval court rolls, parish registers or other contemporary legal documents that name a Lady Eleanor and a Mother Bagden in the precise context Roby gives. In short: there is no published primary medieval document so far identified that proves the prophetic episode as a historical event. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/chapter-i-general-history-pages1-64.pdf))

That distinction matters because it separates two kinds of truth we often conflate in places like Healey Dell: documented, verifiable fact and local storytelling that helps a community make sense of place. The Dell itself is real and recorded — a managed nature reserve on the Spodden with visible industrial archaeology and a striking Victorian railway viaduct now listed on the National Heritage List for England — but the supernatural elements of the tale (a Fairy Queen with prophetic power, an enchantress whose words are fulfilled) belong to folklore. ([planning.data.gov.uk](https://www.planning.data.gov.uk/entity/31773814))

How the story may have formed is straightforward to reconstruct from those sources. A dramatic landscape feature (a cleft called the Fairies’ Chapel), the presence of old mills and families with long feuds, and a local appetite for telling and collecting ghostly or romantic tales supplied the scaffolding. Collectors like Roby were explicitly gathering and reworking oral tradition for print; later local antiquarians then adapted those printed forms into guidebook copy that still circulates to visitors. Where printed folklore meets physical ruins, memory can easily harden into a version that reads like local history. ([redlectern.com](https://redlectern.com/read/traditions-of-lancashire-volume-2))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s collected tale for the earliest popular printed form; examine the Healey Dell guide material for the local, interpretative retelling; and consult manorial and parish histories for the Byron family’s verifiable presence in the area. If anyone hopes to prove the prophecy with a medieval legal record, the printed nineteenth‑century collectors do not cite such a document and none has been produced in the local guides so far. That means the prophecy should be read, for now, as well‑preserved folklore rooted in a vividly atmospheric place rather than as established medieval fact. ([redlectern.com](https://redlectern.com/read/traditions-of-lancashire-volume-2))

articles.excerpt: 6 new stories in the Rochdale borough since yesterday morning.
articles.content_html:
6 new stories in the Rochdale borough since yesterday morning.

The stories

  • Laced vapes: what is in them, how they reach children, and how to report sellers Rochdale
    Vapes sold to children as cannabis oil are being found to contain spice, a far stronger synthetic drug that has put young people in hospital.
  • Rochdale Christmas Toy Appeal aims to deliver 10,000 gifts to children in need Rochdale
    Rochdale Borough Council's Christmas Toy Appeal seeks donations to provide gifts for 3,000 children living in poverty this festive season.
  • Heywood residents praised for Remembrance tributes on Armistice Day Heywood
    Thousands gathered in Heywood and Rochdale to honour war heroes during Remembrance Sunday and Armistice Day commemorations, with heartfelt tributes and moments of silence.
  • Measles: the symptoms to look out for in your child, and when to get help Rochdale
    More than 1,000 measles cases have been confirmed in England this year, 111 of them in the North West. Here is how the illness starts and the warning signs that need urgent care.
  • Rochdale to face York City again after April title decider Rochdale
    Rochdale will meet York City in League Two, marking their first encounter since last season's thrilling title decider in the National League.
  • Rochdale IT provider offers solutions for email disruptions during Microsoft outages Rochdale
    Rochdale-based IT provider No Fuss IT has urged local businesses to consider alternative communication methods in light of recent Microsoft 365 outages that disrupted email services.

Weather: Partly cloudy 7°C in Rochdale today.
